# Phase 2 Results — CNN + BiLSTM + Transformer Ensemble on IoTID20

**Review 2 deliverable** (`PRD.md §8`) · **Task:** T2.6 · **Generated by:** `notebooks/03_train_ensemble_iotid20.ipynb`
**Companion tables:** `reports/t2_6_ensemble_results.csv`, `reports/t2_6_run_metadata.json`

> ### POSITIVE CLASS = **Attack** (label 1)
> Every metric in this document treats **Attack** as the positive class (`TRD.md §2.3`). This is
> deliberately the **opposite** of the base paper, which uses *Normal* as positive — and which, in
> doing so, swaps its own precision and recall labels (`PRD.md §2.1.3`, worked at `PRD.md §10`).
> Every number below was recomputed by hand from the raw confusion-matrix cells and asserted equal
> to scikit-learn's value before being written here.

---

## 1. Summary for a reader in a hurry

Phase 2 delivered what it committed to: a **fully specified** three-branch ensemble over **genuine
flow sequences**, trained on a leakage-free pipeline. Objection #2 is fixed — every layer count,
unit count, and head count is documented in code, in `docs/architecture_decision.md`, and below.

It also produced **two results that contradict the design's expectations**, and this report leads
with them rather than burying them:

1. **The sequence ensemble scores well below the row-level baseline** (F1 0.9439 vs 0.9980). §5
   explains why the two are not directly comparable, and what part of the gap is real.
2. **Confidence-weighted fusion did not beat the alternatives it was chosen over**, and the best
   *single* branch beats all three fusion rules. §6 diagnoses the cause precisely: branch
   confidences are saturated, so the weighting degenerates to a simple average.

Neither is a pleasant result. Both are measured, reproducible, and reported here because a project
whose central contribution is methodological honesty does not get to report only its wins.

---

## 2. What was built (Objection #2, fixed)

The base paper's Table 7 lists three Conv1D layers, ReLU, Adam, dropout, epochs, and batch size —
and **nothing at all** about its LSTM: no unit count, no layer count (`PRD.md §2.1.2`). Its
recurrent component cannot be reproduced by a reader. Here is the equivalent table for this project,
with nothing omitted.

| Branch | Exact architecture | Parameters |
|---|---|---:|
| **CNN** | 3 × Conv1D (**64, 128, 64** filters), kernel **3**, stride 1, padding `same`, **ReLU**, BatchNorm after each, dropout **0.3**, GlobalMaxPooling1D → 64-d | 62,466 |
| **BiLSTM** | **2 layers**, **64 units per direction** (128-d concatenated state), merge `concat`, dropout **0.3**, `recurrent_dropout` **0.0**, Dense(64, ReLU) → 64-d | 172,226 |
| **Transformer** | **2 encoder layers**, **4 attention heads**, key_dim **16**, embed dim **64**, FFN **128**, dropout **0.1**, fixed sinusoidal positions, GlobalAveragePooling1D → 64-d | 71,106 |
| **Fusion** | `c_b = max_k p_b[k]`; `w_b = α_b·c_b^γ / Σ`; `P = Σ w_b·p_b`; **γ = 1.0**, **α_b = 1.0** | 3 (the α vector) |

**Sequence construction** (`TRD.md §3.1`): sessions are per-**destination device** (`Dst_IP`), broken
by a **1.0-second** inactivity gap; window length **10**, training stride **5**, pre-padded, each
window labelled by its **last** record.

**Input shape: `(41284, 10, 62)` = (batch, sequence_length, features).** `sequence_length = 10 > 1`,
asserted in code (`TRD.md §9`'s gate). The base paper's input is a single flow record.

**Training** (`docs/architecture_decision.md` §2.4): Adam(1e-3), categorical cross-entropy, batch
256, max 50 epochs, early stopping on validation **positive-class F1** (patience 5, best weights
restored), seed 42. Converged in 17 / 18 / 28 epochs (21s / 82s / 94s on an Apple-silicon CPU).

---

## 3. Data pipeline

Leakage-free throughout, following `TRD.md §2.2` plus the deduplication that T1.2 §11 showed to be
necessary:

```
clean + deduplicate → sessionise (Dst_IP, 1s gap) → SPLIT BY SESSION (80/10/10)
  → feature-select (training rows only, 83→62) → build windows within each fold
  → min-max scale (training statistics only) → class weights → train
```

| Fold | Sessions | Windows | Share | Attack rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Train | 1,475 | 41,284 | 81.1% | 0.896 |
| Test | 1,315 | 4,894 | 9.6% | 0.871 |
| Validation | 1,452 | 4,700 | 9.2% | — |

**Test fold: 0.00% synthetic rows.** Every evaluated window is real observed traffic.

Two pipeline choices need stating because they are not the obvious defaults:

- **The split is by *session*, never by window.** Adjacent windows in a session share up to 9 of
  their 10 records; splitting windows directly would put near-duplicates on both sides — the exact
  bug this project exists to expose, reintroduced by our own sequence builder. Session assignment is
  additionally **size-aware** (bin-packed largest-first into window quotas), because IoTID20 session
  sizes are so skewed that random assignment produced folds of 98% / 39% / 96% Attack.
- **Imbalance is handled with class weights, not SMOTE.** SMOTE on a flattened 620-dimensional flow
  sequence would fabricate sessions blending two devices' traffic over time — objects that cannot
  occur on a real network, whose timestep dynamics are precisely what the BiLSTM and attention
  branches are meant to learn. Rationale in `src/models/train_utils.py`. **This differs from the
  row-level baseline**, which does use SMOTE, and §5 accounts for it.

## 4. Results

**Positive class = Attack (label 1). All metrics hand-verified against the confusion matrix.**

| Model | Accuracy | Precision | Recall | F1 | TP | FP | TN | FN |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **T1.2 baseline — Random Forest** (records, not sequences) | **0.9964** | **0.9971** | **0.9990** | **0.9980** | 23,376 | 69 | 2,684 | 24 |
| CNN branch alone | 0.8927 | 0.9072 | 0.9768 | 0.9407 | 4,166 | 426 | 203 | 99 |
| BiLSTM branch alone | 0.8674 | 0.8814 | 0.9796 | 0.9279 | 4,178 | 562 | 67 | 87 |
| **Transformer branch alone** | **0.9254** | **0.9408** | 0.9759 | **0.9580** | 4,162 | 262 | 367 | 103 |
| **Ensemble — confidence-weighted fusion** | 0.8982 | 0.9081 | 0.9826 | 0.9439 | 4,191 | 424 | 205 | 74 |
| Fusion baseline — simple average | 0.8980 | 0.9074 | 0.9834 | 0.9439 | 4,194 | 428 | 201 | 71 |
| Fusion baseline — majority vote | 0.8991 | 0.9059 | 0.9866 | 0.9446 | 4,208 | 437 | 192 | 57 |

One property worth noting in the ensemble's favour: it has the **fewest missed attacks of the three
fusion rules bar majority vote** (FN 74) while the best single branch misses 103. In an IoMT
setting a missed attack is the costlier error, so recall — where the ensemble leads every individual
branch — is arguably the more relevant column than F1. That is an argument for the ensemble, not a
rescue of it: its precision is materially worse.

---

## 5. Why the ensemble scores below the row-level baseline

The gap (F1 0.9439 vs 0.9980) is large and must not be waved away. Four factors, in descending order
of how much we can actually attribute to them:

1. **They classify different things.** The baseline labels an individual flow *record*; the ensemble
   labels a 10-record *window*, by its last record. A window whose final record is an attack but
   whose first nine are benign is a genuinely harder call, and a window-level F1 and a record-level
   F1 are simply not the same quantity. **This alone makes the two numbers non-comparable**, and any
   slide showing them side by side must say so.
2. **The evaluation populations differ.** The baseline's test fold is 26,153 records at 89.5% Attack,
   drawn by stratified random split. The ensemble's is 4,894 windows at 87.1% Attack, drawn by
   *session*. Session-level splitting is strictly the more honest design — it is what stops
   overlapping windows leaking — but it also produces a harder, more realistic test fold, because
   entire behavioural episodes are unseen rather than individual records.
3. **Different imbalance handling** (SMOTE vs class weights, §3). This is a real confound that we
   chose deliberately and cannot eliminate without fabricating implausible sequences.
4. **Capacity and training budget.** The Random Forest fits 936k rows unconstrained; the branches see
   41k windows for under 30 epochs on CPU. No hyperparameter search has been run — §2's numbers are
   justified first choices from `docs/architecture_decision.md`, not tuned optima.

**What this does *not* mean.** It does not mean sequence modelling is the wrong approach — the
comparison is not clean enough to support that conclusion, and factors 1 and 2 are structural rather
than evidence about model quality. **What it does mean** is that this project cannot currently claim
its ensemble outperforms a well-built classical baseline on IoTID20, and Review 2 should say exactly
that. A clean comparison requires evaluating both models on the *same* unit and the *same* folds,
which is the first item in §8.

---

## 6. Why confidence-weighted fusion didn't help — diagnosed, not shrugged at

`TRD.md §3.3` requires confidence weighting specifically over a simple average or majority vote. On
this data all three land within 0.0007 F1 of each other. The notebook tests the obvious hypothesis
directly, and confirms it:

| Branch | Mean confidence | **Median confidence** | Share > 0.99 | **Mean fusion weight** |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| CNN | 0.9698 | **0.9999** | 79.3% | **0.3366** |
| BiLSTM | 0.9549 | **0.9993** | 74.7% | **0.3299** |
| Transformer | 0.9640 | **0.9998** | 78.4% | **0.3336** |

Mean per-sample spread between the most and least confident branch: **0.0600**.

**The fusion weights are 0.337 / 0.330 / 0.334 — indistinguishable from a uniform 1/3.** The formula
is working exactly as specified; it is being fed an input it cannot use. Every branch declares
near-certainty on nearly every window, so `c_b^γ` is effectively constant and the weighted sum
collapses into the simple average it was chosen to beat.

A sweep over γ from 0 to 64 confirms this is not a tuning problem: F1 rises only from 0.9439 (γ=1)
to **0.9489** at γ=64, still well short of the Transformer's 0.9580. Sharpening weights that are
built on uninformative confidences cannot recover information that was never there.

**The real defect is branch calibration, not the fusion rule.** Over-parameterised softmax
classifiers are known to be badly calibrated, and these are no exception. That is a specific,
fixable problem with a standard remedy (temperature scaling per branch, fitted on the validation
fold), and it is recorded in §8 as a Phase 3 proposal — **not** implemented now, because it is not in
the frozen `docs/architecture_decision.md` §3.1 and quietly adding it mid-phase would be precisely
the undocumented drift this project criticises in the base paper.

## 8. What Phase 3 should do about all this

1. **Make one clean comparison.** Evaluate the Random Forest baseline on the *same* windowed test
   fold as the ensemble. Until that exists, §4's first row and the rest of the table are measuring
   different things and cannot settle whether sequence modelling helps.
2. **Calibrate the branches** (temperature scaling on the validation fold) and re-measure fusion.
   §6 predicts this is what makes confidence weighting do any work at all.
3. **Fit `α_b` instead of leaving all three at 1.0.** T3.5's incremental-learning mechanism already
   updates exactly this vector — the fusion layer's only adjustable parameter — so letting the
   Transformer earn a larger prior needs no architectural change and no new spec.
4. **Report single-branch results in `ablation_study.md` (T4.4).** On IoTID20 the honest headline is
   that the best single branch beats the ensemble; the ablation must say so plainly.
5. **Re-run the GNN sparsity check on Edge-IIoTset** (T3.6) rather than assuming IoTID20's verdict
   carries over.

---

## 9. Standing caveats

- **IoTID20's sessions are 100% label-pure**, because each attack scenario was captured separately.
  A window therefore never straddles the benign/attack boundary — easier than a live deployment,
  where an attack begins mid-session. **This inflates every sequence result in §4** relative to
  reality. Edge-IIoTset (T3.6) is the check on how much.
- **58.2% of cleaned IoTID20 rows are exact duplicates.** All results here are post-deduplication.
  Neither the base paper nor the senior's prior work mentions this, and it is a larger leakage vector
  than the SMOTE-ordering bug that motivated Contribution 1 (T1.2 §11).
- **No hyperparameter search has been run.** §2's values are justified first choices, not optima.
- **No latency or throughput number appears anywhere in this document**, because no measurement on
  the Raspberry Pi 4B exists yet (T4.3). Nothing here supports a real-time claim.
- **The base paper's headline numbers are deliberately absent.** Where T4.4 does cite HIDS-IoMT's
  99.92% / 99.91% / 99.99% / 99.95%, the metric-inversion caveat (`PRD.md §10`) must appear in the
  same paragraph. Those numbers are the object of a critique, not a target.

## 10. Reproducing

```bash
python scripts/download_data.py
jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --inplace notebooks/03_train_ensemble_iotid20.ipynb
```

Seed 42 throughout, with TensorFlow op determinism enabled. Environment pinned in
`requirements.txt`, which records its two deviations from `TRD.md §8` and why.
